lessons.title: The Innate Compass (Fitrah)
lessons.objective: Identify the Qur'anic concept of fitrah as humanity's innate orientation toward truth.
lessons.hook: Why do people across every culture share an instinctive pull toward fairness, awe, and meaning?

sources.author: The Qur'an
sources.translator: Ali Quli Qara'i (Qara'i translation, via Tanzil)
sources.quote: So set your heart as a person of pure faith on this religion, the original nature endowed by Allah according to which He originated mankind

lessons.summary: Surah al-Rum 30:30 grounds human spirituality in fitrah, the original nature created by God, inviting learners to recognize truth as something deeply aligned with human nature.

questions.prompt: According to 30:30, what is fitrah?
options: The original nature endowed by Allah
A habit picked up from the surroundings
A rule agreed by a community
questions.explanation: The verse calls it the original nature endowed by Allah, according to which He originated mankind.

questions.prompt: Match the root f-t-r (fitrah) to its meaning in this lesson.
questions.explanation: In this verse fitrah means the original nature, not something learned from outside.

lessons.title: Wisdom, Refinement & Consultation
lessons.objective: Contrast lasting inner wealth (wisdom and refinement) with ignorance, and recognize consultation as a core support.
lessons.hook: If you lost all your possessions tomorrow, what kind of wealth would still protect your judgment?

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: There is no wealth like wisdom, no destitution like ignorance, no inheritance like refinement and no support like consultation.

lessons.summary: Saying 54 teaches that wisdom outweighs material wealth, ignorance is the deepest poverty, refined character is the finest inheritance, and seeking counsel is the strongest support.
lessons.familyNote: Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib frames consultation and wisdom as practical anchors for everyday decisions (Saying 54).

questions.prompt: In Saying 54, which is called the strongest support?
questions.explanation: The saying says there is no support like consultation.

questions.prompt: You face a big life decision and feel the urge to act at once. Which choice fits Saying 54?
options: Ask people of sound judgment for counsel first
questions.explanation: Saying 54 treats consultation as the strongest support.

lessons.title: The Formula Against Loss
lessons.objective: Identify the themes of Surah al-'Asr (103:1-3): faith, righteous action, truth, and patience.
lessons.hook: What four habits separate a life well spent from one that slips away?

sources.author: The Qur'an
sources.translator: Ali Quli Qara'i (Qara'i translation, via Tanzil)
sources.quote: By Time! Man is indeed in loss, except those who have faith and do righteous deeds, and enjoin one another to [follow] the truth, and enjoin one another to patience.

lessons.summary: Surah al-'Asr 103:1-3 links faith and righteous deeds with mutually encouraging one another to truth and patience.

questions.prompt: Which four things does Surah al-'Asr name as the way out of loss?
options: Faith, righteous deeds, urging one another to truth, urging one another to patience
questions.explanation: The verse lists faith, righteous deeds, and enjoining truth and patience on one another.

questions.prompt: A friend is discouraged and wants to give up a good habit. Which response matches 103:3?
options: Encourage them gently to patience and to hold to what is true
Tell them it is their own business
questions.explanation: The surah describes people who enjoin one another to truth and patience.

lessons.title: Pure Oneness (Surah al-Ikhlas)
lessons.objective: Study Surah al-Ikhlas (112:1-4) as the Qur'an's concise statement of divine oneness.
lessons.hook: How do you speak about an infinite Creator without shrinking God into a human-sized image?

sources.author: The Qur'an
sources.translator: Ali Quli Qara'i (Qara'i translation, via Tanzil)
sources.quote: Say, ‘He is Allah, the One. Allah is the All-embracing. He neither begat, nor was begotten, nor has He any equal.’

lessons.summary: Surah al-Ikhlas 112:1-4 presents God's absolute unity and incomparability in four brief verses.

questions.prompt: Which statement is in Surah al-Ikhlas?
options: He neither begat, nor was begotten, nor has He any equal
He has a partner in creation
He is one of many powers
questions.explanation: Verse 4 says He neither begat, nor was begotten, nor has any equal.

questions.prompt: Which idea do the words 'nor has He any equal' clear away?
options: That anything in creation is God's equal
questions.explanation: If nothing is His equal, no creature can be set beside Him.

candidates: Paired with NAHJ Sermon 1 in lessons 1.2.2-1.2.3.

lessons.title: With Everything, Beyond Physical Limits
lessons.objective: Explain how Imam Ali describes God's nearness without physical contact and distinction without physical distance.
lessons.hook: If God is not a physical object in a location, what does it mean to say God is close to everything?

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: He is with everything but not in physical nearness. He is different from everything but not in physical separation.

sources.author: The Qur'an
sources.translator: Ali Quli Qara'i (Qara'i translation, via Tanzil)
sources.quote: Nothing is like Him, and He is the All-hearing, the All-seeing.

lessons.summary: Sermon 1 teaches that God is present with all creation without being physically attached to it, and utterly distinct from creation without being physically distant.
lessons.familyNote: Imam Ali opens Nahj al-Balagha by clearing away physical analogies for God so learners approach Tawhid with clarity (Sermon 1).

questions.prompt: In Sermon 1, God is 'with everything'. In what way?
options: By living in one place in the sky
questions.explanation: The sermon says He is with everything but not in physical nearness.

questions.prompt: Which way of speaking about God accidentally suggests a physical place?
options: 'God sits up in the clouds, far from us'
'God is with everything, but not in physical nearness'
questions.explanation: Sitting somewhere implies physical space, which the sermon sets aside.

lessons.title: Acknowledgement Leads to Testimony
lessons.objective: Explain why Nahj al-Balagha Sermon 1 calls acknowledging God the starting point of religion rather than the end.
lessons.hook: Why isn't privately agreeing that God exists the finish line of faith?

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: The foremost in religion is the acknowledgement of Him, the perfection of acknowledging Him is to testify Him

lessons.summary: Sermon 1 states that religion begins with acknowledging God and matures when that acknowledgement becomes genuine testimony.
lessons.familyNote: Imam Ali sets out a progressive path of knowing God in Sermon 1, moving from initial recognition to wholehearted affirmation.

questions.prompt: Put the progression in Sermon 1 in order.
items: Acknowledging God is the first step of religion
It reaches perfection as genuine testimony
questions.explanation: Religion begins with acknowledgement, and its perfection is to testify.

questions.prompt: According to Sermon 1, what comes first in religion?
questions.explanation: The foremost in religion is the acknowledgement of Him.

lessons.title: The Courage to Say "I Do Not Know"
lessons.objective: Practice intellectual honesty by admitting when you do not know an answer.
lessons.hook: When someone asks you a hard question you genuinely cannot answer, why is guessing worse than saying "I don't know"?

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: no one should feel ashamed of saying 'I do not know' when he is asked a matter which he does not know

lessons.summary: Saying 82 removes any stigma from admitting ignorance, teaching that honest humility is preferable to pretending to know.
lessons.familyNote: Imam Ali models epistemic humility as a foundational habit for every learner (Saying 82).

questions.prompt: A friend asks you an obscure question about Islam you cannot answer. What does Saying 82 point you to?
options: Say honestly that you do not know
questions.explanation: No one should feel ashamed of saying 'I do not know'.

questions.prompt: What does Saying 82 say about admitting you do not know?
options: No one should be ashamed of it
It is a sign of weakness
questions.explanation: The saying removes the shame from honest ignorance.

lessons.title: Testing What You Hear
lessons.objective: Apply intelligence and reflection when evaluating a reported statement rather than repeating it uncritically.
lessons.hook: When a dramatic religious quote goes viral online, what should you do before sharing it?

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: When you hear a tradition test it according to the criterion of intelligence not that of mere hearing

lessons.summary: Saying 98 urges learners to examine what they hear with active understanding and intelligence rather than passively repeating words.
lessons.familyNote: Imam Ali distinguishes thoughtful comprehension from uncritical repetition (Saying 98).

questions.prompt: By what criterion should you test a tradition, according to Saying 98?
questions.explanation: The saying says to use the criterion of intelligence, not mere hearing.

questions.prompt: A dramatic quote is going viral. Which response matches Saying 98?
options: Pause and examine it with understanding before passing it on
Share it only if it moves you
questions.explanation: Saying 98 asks for active understanding rather than repeating words.

lessons.title: Heart, Tongue, and Limbs
lessons.objective: Define belief (iman) through the three aligned dimensions taught in Nahj al-Balagha Saying 227.
lessons.hook: Is belief only an inner feeling, or does it require alignment between thoughts, words, and actions?

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: Belief means appreciation with the heart, acknowledgement with the tongue, and action with the limbs.

lessons.summary: Saying 227 defines belief as a three-part whole: inner appreciation in the heart, honest expression on the tongue, and lived action through the limbs.
lessons.familyNote: Imam Ali reinforces this idea of belief as inner conviction joined to action.

questions.prompt: In Saying 227, what is done with the heart?
questions.explanation: Belief is appreciation with the heart.

questions.prompt: Which daily example matches 'action with the limbs'?
options: Helping a neighbour carry heavy shopping
Saying you care without doing anything
questions.explanation: Action with the limbs means belief shown through what you do.

candidates: NAHJ Saying 125 as a family note: the syllabus text contains an ellipsis; split into exact quotes before use.

lessons.title: Created Free
lessons.objective: Recognize human freedom and moral independence as a God-given dignity.
lessons.hook: What social pressures or expectations quietly make people act like they belong to others instead of standing in their own dignity?

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: Do not be the slave of others for Allah had made you free.

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: the heart of a young man is like uncultivated land. It accepts whatever is strewn on it.

lessons.summary: Letter 31 reminds young readers never to surrender their dignity to others, because God created every human being free.
lessons.familyNote: In the same fatherly letter (Letter 31), Imam Ali writes about the open heart of the young.

questions.prompt: Why does Letter 31 say not to be the slave of others?
options: Because Allah had made you free
questions.explanation: The letter gives the reason: Allah had made you free.

questions.prompt: Peer pressure pushes you to do something you disagree with. Which response keeps dignity and kindness?
questions.explanation: Letter 31 asks you not to give up your dignity to others, without calling for unkindness.

lessons.title: The Worship of Free People
lessons.objective: Identify gratitude as the motivation behind what Saying 237 calls "the worship of free men."
lessons.hook: What is the difference between doing good to get a reward, doing good out of fear, and doing good out of gratitude?

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: Still another group worshipped Allah out of gratefulness; this is the worship of free men.

lessons.summary: Saying 237 highlights gratitude as the highest posture of devotion, describing worship offered out of thankfulness as the worship of free people.
lessons.familyNote: Imam Ali elevates gratitude above fear or transaction as the hallmark of spiritual maturity (Saying 237).

questions.prompt: What does Saying 237 call worship offered out of gratefulness?
questions.explanation: The saying calls it the worship of free men.

questions.prompt: Which motivation reflects gratitude-driven devotion?
options: Doing good because you feel thankful
Doing good only to earn a reward
questions.explanation: Gratitude, not fear or reward, is the motive Saying 237 highlights.

lessons.title: Tier 1 Checkpoint: Two Kinds of Humanity
lessons.objective: Apply Letter 53's principle of universal human dignity across faith and background.
lessons.hook: How should you treat someone who does not share your religious beliefs?

sources.author: Compiled by al-Sharif al-Radi
sources.quote: they are of two kinds, either your brother in religion or one like you in creation.

lessons.summary: Letter 53 instructs that every person belongs to one of two bonds, fellowship in faith or equality in shared human creation, establishing universal respect.
lessons.familyNote: Imam Ali wrote this directive as a public-service principle for governing a diverse population with fairness (Letter 53).
